passages.happening:
Joseph hears that his father is ill and comes with his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim (verse 1). “Israel rallied his strength and sat up in bed” (verse 2).

Jacob remembers: “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and there He blessed me” (verse 3). God promised to make him “a multitude of peoples” and to give the land to his descendants “as an everlasting possession” (verse 4).

Then he says, “your two sons born to you in Egypt before I came to you here shall be reckoned as mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine” (verse 5). Any later children will be Joseph's own (verse 6).

And he remembers Rachel. She “died along the way in the land of Canaan, some distance from Ephrath. So I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Luz is the old name of Bethel (28:19). There Jacob dreamed of the stairway to heaven, and there God met him again on his way home (35:9-12). Before he says anything else, the dying man goes back to God's promise.

Then he adopts his grandsons. To ‘reckon’ them as his means they will count as his own sons, with full shares, just like Reuben and Simeon, his two eldest. In this way Joseph receives a double share: two tribes instead of one. Israel's law later gave the firstborn a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17). Reuben was the firstborn, but he lost his place (35:22). Joseph, the firstborn of Rachel, receives it.

Why does he speak of Rachel here? Perhaps because Joseph and these boys are all he has left of her. Perhaps because Rachel died on the road, never reaching the place where he hoped to settle, and he wants Joseph to know where she lies. Rachel had only two sons. By adopting Joseph's two, Jacob gives her, in a way, the larger family she longed for.

The narrator adds that Ephrath is Bethlehem. Another verse places Rachel's tomb near Zelzah on Benjamin's border (1 Samuel 10:2). The note on 35:16-20 sets out the question; it is open.
passages.later:
The Chronicler explains how it came out: Reuben's “birthright was given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel, because Reuben defiled his father's bed” (1 Chronicles 5:1). “And though Judah prevailed over his brothers and a ruler came from him, the birthright belonged to Joseph” (1 Chronicles 5:2).

Matthew recalls Rachel's grief near Bethlehem: “Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more” (Matthew 2:18).
passages.asks: Jacob took two boys born in a foreign land and made them his own sons. Ask whether you know what it is to be welcomed into a family where you did not seem to belong. Then ask who you could welcome in that way.

passages.happening:
“When Israel saw the sons of Joseph, he asked, ‘Who are these?’” (verse 8). “They are the sons God has given me in this place,” Joseph says (verse 9). Jacob asks him to bring them close, “that I may bless them” (verse 9).

“Now Israel's eyesight was poor because of old age; he could hardly see” (verse 10). He kisses the boys and embraces them.

“I never expected to see your face again,” Israel said to Joseph, “but now God has let me see your children as well” (verse 11).

Joseph takes his sons from his father's knees “and bowed facedown” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers would hear an old story in this one. Long ago Isaac was old and almost blind when he blessed his sons (27:1). Isaac asked, “Which one are you, my son?” (27:18), and was tricked into blessing the younger. Now Jacob, the son who tricked his father, is the old man who can hardly see.

But this time no one is deceived. Jacob asks who the boys are, and Joseph tells him plainly.

Listen to Joseph's answer: ‘the sons God has given me in this place.’ Joseph named these boys in his grief and his new life. Manasseh means ‘making forget’, and Ephraim means ‘fruitful’ (41:51-52). He calls them God's gifts, given in Egypt.

And listen to Jacob: ‘I never expected to see your face again, but now God has let me see your children as well.’ He had said he would go down to the grave mourning (37:35). God gave him more than he dared to hope.

The boys are on Jacob's knees. Setting children on one's knees was a way of receiving them as one's own. Rachel used the same picture for Bilhah's children (30:3). Joseph will one day have his great-grandchildren on his knees (50:23).
passages.later:
Paul writes that God “is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine” (Ephesians 3:20).

A psalm prays for the blessing Jacob now sees, a long life, “that you may see your children's children” (Psalm 128:6).
passages.asks: Jacob thought he had lost his son for ever, and God let him hold his grandsons. Ask whether there is a loss you have stopped hoping about. Then ask whether you can leave room for God to give more than you expect.

passages.happening:
Joseph brings the boys forward, Manasseh to his father's right hand and Ephraim to his left (verse 13). “But Israel stretched out his right hand and put it on the head of Ephraim, the younger; and crossing his hands, he put his left on Manasseh's head, although Manasseh was the firstborn” (verse 14).

He blesses them: “May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all harm” bless these boys (verses 15-16).

Joseph is displeased and tries to move his father's hand. “Not so, my father!” he says. “This one is the firstborn” (verse 18).

“But his father refused. ‘I know, my son, I know!’” (verse 19). Manasseh will be great, “nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he” (verse 19). “So he put Ephraim before Manasseh” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The right hand was the hand of honor and strength. The firstborn expected it. Joseph places the boys carefully so that Manasseh, the elder, stands at his grandfather's right. Jacob has to cross his arms to reverse them.

This is a pattern all through Genesis: the younger chosen over the older. Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Perez over Zerah, Joseph over his elder brothers. Now Ephraim over Manasseh. God's choice rests on grace, not on order of birth. The book page on Genesis lists this among its big themes.

But notice the difference from chapter 27. There, the younger son was blessed by a trick. Here the old man knows exactly what he is doing. ‘I know, my son, I know.’

The blessing is a short poem with three names for God. He is the God before whom the fathers walked. He is ‘my shepherd’, who has cared for Jacob all his life. And he is ‘the angel who has redeemed me from all harm’. To redeem is to rescue or buy back. Jacob looks back over a hard life and sees that God carried him through it all.

The blessing lived on. ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh’ (verse 20) is still spoken by many Jewish parents over their sons on Friday evening, as the Sabbath begins.

In Israel's history Ephraim did become the greater tribe. Joshua came from Ephraim (Numbers 13:8). So did Jeroboam, first king of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 11:26). The prophets often call the whole northern kingdom ‘Ephraim’.
passages.later:
Hebrews names this moment as an act of faith: “By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph's sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff” (Hebrews 11:21). Genesis 47:31 says he bowed at the head of his ‘bed’. In Hebrew, ‘bed’ and ‘staff’ are written with the same letters; the old Greek translation read ‘staff’, and Hebrews follows it.

Hosea uses the tribe's name for all the northern kingdom: “How could I give you up, O Ephraim?” (Hosea 11:8). And Jesus took up the name Jacob used for God: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).
passages.hard:
Why does God keep choosing the younger over the older? Is it fair to the firstborn?

In that world the firstborn had a natural claim to lead the family and to inherit more. By passing over that claim again and again, Genesis shows that God's blessing is a gift, not a right. His plans do not depend on human rank.

Christians read the pattern in more than one way. Paul uses God's choice of Jacob over Esau to show that God's call is “not by works but by Him who calls” (Romans 9:12). Many in the Reformed tradition read that passage as God choosing individuals for salvation. Others read the choices in Genesis as God choosing peoples or persons for a role in history, not a verdict on anyone's eternal future. The note on 25:19-26 sets out these readings, and these notes take no side.

On every reading, the one passed over is not thrown away. “He too shall become a people, and he too shall be great” (verse 19), Jacob says of Manasseh.
passages.asks: Jacob crossed his hands on purpose and would not be corrected. Ask whether you resent the way God's gifts are given to others, or to you. Then ask what it would mean to receive your place as grace, not as a right.

passages.happening:
“Then Israel said to Joseph, ‘Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers’” (verse 21).

“And to you, as one who is above your brothers, I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Jacob is dying in Egypt, but his eyes are on Canaan. ‘God will be with you and bring you back.’ It is the same promise God gave him at Beersheba (46:4). He hands it on to his son.

The ‘ridge of land’ is, in Hebrew, one word: shekem, which means ‘shoulder’. It sounds like Shechem, the town. Many readers think Jacob means land at Shechem. Jacob had bought a plot of ground there (33:19). Later Joseph's bones were buried in that very plot (Joshua 24:32).

But Jacob says he took this land ‘with my sword and bow’. Genesis tells no such battle. It tells of Simeon and Levi killing the men of Shechem (chapter 34), which Jacob condemned. Some readers think Jacob speaks here of a fight the book does not record. Others think he counts his sons' deed as the family's act, though he condemned it. The text does not settle it.

Whatever the land was, the gift is a sign of the promise. Joseph's family will have a place in Canaan.
passages.later:
Joshua tells how the promise was kept: “the bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up out of Egypt, were buried at Shechem in the plot of land that Jacob had purchased from the sons of Hamor” (Joshua 24:32).

Centuries later Jesus sat by a well “near the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph” (John 4:5).
passages.asks: Jacob gave Joseph a piece of land he would not see for many years. Ask what you are handing on to the next generation: things to use now, or a promise to wait for. Then ask what promise of God you would want your children to carry.
